Interpretation with SLOOS overlay

- Policy stance: The FOMC held the target range at 5.25–5.50% and kept balance sheet runoff on pace (Treasury cap $60B/month; agency MBS cap $35B). IORB at 5.4% and ON RRP at 5.3% remain the main operating tools. Cuts require “greater confidence” that inflation is moving sustainably to 2%.
- Macro tone: Real activity is solid, job gains strong, and inflation has eased but is still elevated. Risks to employment and inflation are moving toward better balance, with the Committee highly attentive to inflation risks.

SLOOS-informed credit conditions
- Large banks reported weaker demand for C&I loans, indicating softer private credit appetite/investment.
- Banks tightened standards on commercial real estate (CRE) loans; foreign banks also reported tighter CRE standards, underscoring ongoing stress in offices and related segments.
- Residential real estate: Standards tightened across non-GSE/QM segments (including non-QM jumbo and other non-GSE-eligible mortgages), while GSE-eligible mortgage standards were broadly unchanged—credit remains selectively restrictive.
- Households: Auto loans saw tighter standards, pointing to constrained consumer credit at the margin.
- Stated reasons for tightening include the economic outlook, risk considerations, and liquidity/capital positions.

Implications for policy tone
- The SLOOS points to restrictive credit supply and weak loan demand in key areas (C&I, CRE, non-GSE mortgages, auto), which should act as a headwind to growth and inflation.
- This tempers the otherwise cautiously hawkish FOMC language: restrictive credit reduces the need for additional tightening and supports patience while waiting for clearer disinflation.
- Net read: balanced-to-cautiously hawkish, with a modest dovish adjustment versus a statement-only read due to tight credit conditions shown in SLOOS.
